name: California Water Service
headline: A regulated water monopoly: by law, no competitor may serve the areas it already covers.
what_it_does: California Water Service pumps or buys water and pipes it to about 562,000 connections. 91.2% of its revenue comes from its California districts, with small operations in Washington, New Mexico, Hawaii and Texas. The California Public Utilities Commission sets the prices it may charge.
why_it_passed: State law bars any other private water company from entering its territory unless service there is found to be deficient.
The pipes in the street cannot practically be duplicated, and no substitute for piped water is named in its annual report.
The regulator has allowed a steady 10.27% return on equity, with 53.4% equity in the capital structure, unchanged since 2023.
It plans $580 to $640 million of investment in 2026, which grows the base on which it earns its allowed return.
why_not_now: A regulator caps what this utility may earn, so the price is far above what that capped return justifies. At $47.82 a share the price is about double the analysis's value range of $22.60 to $27.66, and even the best case earns only 4.19% a year, against 5.30% on a 30-year US Treasury bond.
watch: Spending on pipes ($517 million in 2025) is far above depreciation and above what the business generates, so it keeps borrowing; debt was about 3.1 times its earnings before interest and tax over interest in 2025.
California holds utilities strictly liable for damage in some cases, even without fault, and land-movement lawsuits are pending.
A public agency could take over the system by eminent domain for just compensation, though only one small case was pending.
